g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=3) Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have recently emerged as a dominant paradigm in vision–language understanding, demonstrating strong performance across tasks such as captioning (Jia et al., 2024), visual question answering (Awadalla et al., 2023), and even visual mathematical reasoning (Chen et al., 2025).

g.text: A common design represents visual input as sequences of visual tokens that
are fed into a generative Large Language Model (LLM) which, after joint
fine-tuning, enables open-world reasoning and instruction following over
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=0) A common design represents visual input as sequences of visual tokens that are fed into a generative Large Language Model (LLM) which, after joint fine-tuning, enables open-world reasoning and instruction following over multimodal content.

g.text: Extending this paradigm from images to videos has led to rapid progress in

g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=5) Extending this paradigm from images to videos has led to rapid progress in video-based MLLMs (Zhang et al., 2024b; Cheng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Tang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025).

g.text: Compared to images, videos introduce richer content and temporal dynamics,

g.title: N4 [Context] (cites=0) Compared to images, videos introduce richer content and temporal dynamics, substantially increasing the challenge of representation learning, reasoning, and retrieval.

g.text: As MLLMs become increasingly widespread, multimodal representation learning
g.title: N5 [Context] (cites=0) As MLLMs become increasingly widespread, multimodal representation learning has attracted growing research interest.

g.title: N6 [Prior_Work] (cites=3) Early vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), ALIGN (Jia et al., 2021), and BLIP (Li et al., 2022) established a powerful dual-encoder recipe for text-image representations by aligning image and text embeddings with contrastive learning on large-scale image-text data.

g.title: N9 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) InternVideo2 (Wang et al., 2024) has pretrained ∼100M video–text pairs to reach superior performance, while VideoPrism (Zhao et al., 2024) contrastively trained with ∼600M pairs.

g.title: N10 [Limitation] (cites=3) Recent studies suggest that simply scaling video–text pretraining does not uniformly improve performance (Feichtenhofer et al., 2022; Tong et al., 2022; Uselis et al., 2025) motivating alternative approaches that focus on representation quality and task-related alignment, rather than relying solely on ever-larger corpora.

g.title: N15 [Limitation] (cites=9) Although recent methods report impressive results on image retrieval (Zhang et al., 2025b; Thirukovalluru et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2026), video is often treated as an auxiliary modality rather than a primary focus, and performance on video retrieval remains behind that of dedicated Video Foundation Models (VFMs) (Wang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023; Lan et al., 2025b).

g.title: N16a [Limitation: example] (cites=3) CARE (Xu et al., 2024) emphasizes fine-grained captioning and retrieval but underperforms in conventional retrieval settings, while VLM2Vec-V2 (Meng et al., 2025) incorporates video–text pairs during training yet reports substantially lower performance, even compared to earlier MLLM-based embedders (Kong et al., 2025).

g.title: N17 [Method] (cites=0) Overview of our approach. In this work, we study MLLMs as embedding extractors specifically for video–text retrieval.

g.title: N22 [Result] (cites=0) Using only ∼60K text-only in-context pairs, we outperform trained MLLM embedders and video foundation models trained on orders of magnitude more video–text data.

g.text: 1. We propose a methodology to assess and exploit
hidden representations of Video MLLMs for video–text
retrieval, and show that intermediate layers can be
markedly more effective than the final layer.
g.title: N23a [Contribution: Contribution 1] (cites=0) 1. We propose a methodology to assess and exploit hidden representations of Video MLLMs for video–text retrieval, and show that intermediate layers can be markedly more effective than the final layer.

g.title: N23b [Contribution: Contribution 2] (cites=0) 2. We introduce an effective zero-shot scheme that leverages the MLLM head as a calibrated likelihood scorer, turning off-the-shelf Video MLLMs into competitive video–text retrievers.

g.title: N23c [Contribution: Contribution 3] (cites=0) 3. We present an efficient in-context optimization strategy that maps dense video captions to short summaries, enabling task-related embedding learning without visual supervision.

g.title: N23d [Contribution: Contribution 4] (cites=0) 4. Without any fine-tuning beyond text, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on common video retrieval benchmarks.

g.text: Figure 1. An overview of VidVec. (a) Zero-shot retrieval: extract video and
text embeddings from an intermediate MLLM layer for initial ranking. (b)
Zero-shot reranking: leverage the calibrated MLLM head for pairwise scoring
g.title: P1 [Proof] (cites=0) Figure 1. An overview of VidVec. (a) Zero-shot retrieval: extract video and text embeddings from an intermediate MLLM layer for initial ranking. (b) Zero-shot reranking: leverage the calibrated MLLM head for pairwise scoring to rerank top-K candidates. (c) In-context optimization: lightweight model alignment using only ∼60K text-only pairs for embedding extraction via a text-to-text mapping from dense video captions to short summaries, designed to mirror the video–text inference setup.
